source: «The DeFranceschi Family Tree Album», compiled for the first family reunion at Crystal Springs Resort, 7–9 September 2012, and its accompanying chart «The Generations of DeFranceschi (2012)». Held by the family; a copy is in this archive's own papers.

children.story: Married Marta Comisso; five children, four sons and a daughter.
children.check: FamilySearch has an Anthony de Franceschi born 18 February 1887 at Gallignana, with a wife Marta — the same day, the same village. Findmypast: a de Franceschi Antonio born 1887 on a United States passenger list in 1922 — the same year his sister Albina crossed.

children.story: Left Gallignana young and was not heard from again.
Left Gallignana young and was not heard from again. An unusual name; nothing has been found under it anywhere.
Emigrated to New York and married Mary Vidovich; a son Joseph and a daughter Doris. Grandfather to Stephen, Daniel and Gary.
children.check: A Joseph Defranceschi born 12 March 1892 at Gallignana appears in the American records; an obituary in the same set names Mary Vidovich Defranceschi and sons Steven, Daniel and Gary. Findmypast: a Defranceschi Joseph born 1892 in the New York naturalisation petitions three times over — 1912, 1915 and 1916.

children.story: Married Giovanni Marfan; four children, three daughters and a son. It was Virginia who received the American cousins at Gallignana in 1972.
Married Frank Chinkopan; no children. She was known in the family as «Everybody's Aunt», and lived in Brooklyn.
children.check: An Albina «Schinkepen or De Franceschi» born 14 April 1900 at Gallignana, with a Frank, is in the American immigration records. Findmypast: a de Franceschi Albina born 1900 on a United States passenger list in 1922.

children.story: Died as a child, in an accident.

The album says he married Albina Chinkopan and left Gallignana for Argentina with two daughters. The register gives him as «Rutilius 3-11-1902, married 16-5-1928» and does not mark him as gone to America; and the Albina who married a Chinkopan turns out to be his own sister. Argentina has been searched and has no Rotilio of this surname.
children.check: Born 3 November 1902, not 1903 — the Status Animarum of 1925, house 24. See «The household reassembles in Brooklyn» below: the one detail the album gave him belongs to his sister, and he is now the least evidenced of the eleven.

children.story: Married Paola Eriavaz. Left Gallignana for Italy in 1947 — the year of the treaty — and settled in Tuscany. Six children, two sons and four daughters.
children.check: 1947 is the year of the Paris peace treaty, which put Gallignana in Yugoslavia. He is one of the 350,000.

children.story: Sailed for America, settled in the New York area, married Gerda Seedorf, one son. He made a tape of the family genealogy and began sending it round the cousins — the first version of the work this page rests on.
children.check: Buried at Nine Partners Cemetery, Millbrook, Dutchess County, New York; Gerda Seedorf de Franceschi, 1913–2012, lies beside him. His is the only located grave of anyone born in this parish. Findmypast closes the gravestone. Bruno de Franceschi born 1907 petitions for citizenship at New York in 1939, and again in 1942 indexed as «Bruno de Franceschi Or Seedorf»; a Gerda de Franceschi born 1913 petitions at New York in the same year, 1939, and again in 1944. The surname the Millbrook stone cut off is SEEDORF.

children.story: The last of the eleven. Followed his brother Bruno to New York with his wife Maria Rovina and two sons.
children.check: His son Dario, born at Gallignana 26 September 1937, died in 1991; his son Benito, born 8 October 1938 or 1939, died 10 February 2022 and is buried at the National Memorial Cemetery of Arizona. Findmypast: Basilio, Dario and Benito de Franceschi all on United States passenger lists in 1955 and 1956 — a father and two sons crossing inside eighteen months.

arms: The house in Moncalvo still stands with its emblem — a shield with a silver turnip in a green leaf on a red background. In the lower part in a silver background, there is a red cross held by a line and crossed by two arrows. The stone shield is hard to read now due to wear and weather.

album.heading: What the album says, read whole
album.lead: This archive had the chart. The seven-page album that came with it had never been read here — it has no text layer and needed to be turned back into images first. It is worth the trouble, because the American branch, who had never seen Carlo De Franceschi's letters to Kobler, tell the same origin story.

rows.lab: The same road, told by people who never read Carlo
rows.text: «The name deFranceschi traces back to the 16th century in the province of Florence, from where some of the offsprings moved to the Northeast corner of Italy known as CARNIA, later it became part of Friuli. Some of the people became farmers, others became artisans of which there was great need at the time. Some of them moved to Aquileia where they entered religious life. More were on the move to the peninsula of Istria in the town of MONCALVO, where Gian Battista deFranceschi built a house in 1711. Through the years he became a fairly wealthy landowner, shopkeeper and trader.» Carnia, the artisans, the 1711 house and Gian Battista: the same four things Carlo wrote privately to Kobler in the 1870s, and which this archive has spent a year corroborating from headmen's lists and notarial inventories. Two branches of one family, separated for a century, carrying the same account.

rows.lab: And the men in between
rows.text: «There was his son Gian Pietro and other DeFranceschi's through the 1800s, Filippo, Gian Mattia who became Parish priests and also Giuseppe, Giuseppe Jr., Carlo, and Camillo.» Gian Pietro is the Giampietro of Carlo's account. And Gian Mattia the parish priest is the man the Visitation of the diocese of Pedena names on 7 April 1788 as «parroco Mattia Defranceschi» of Gologorica, and who signs the register «Ego Joannes Mathias Franceschi Parochus».

rows.lab: Where the birth dates came from
rows.text: «Since there were no birth certificates we could only get birth dates from the 3 churches in Gallignana, San Vito, Santa Eufemia, and Our Lady of the Square.» Three churches named, in the parish this line comes from. The album adds that a cousin who visited years earlier brought back further dates, and that for the reunion all marriages and deaths were left out — «there is still a great deal of work to be done in the future».

rows.lab: The house they were raised in
rows.text: «Grandpa Antonio & Grandma Maria brought 11 children into the world in a 2 bedroom house with an additional room below (a cantina now), with some land to farm, a small vineyard to grow wine, no running water (a pump in the kitchen), no refrigeration, only an ice box, no central heating or air conditioning, and last but not least no bathroom in the house.» Eleven children, two bedrooms, and a pump at the sink.

rows.lab: And it is still lived in
rows.text: The writer first went to Gallignana in 1972 and was received in the house; years later she was given lunch there again, and the afternoon was spent under the grape arbour with the family news. «From medieval times to the 21st century there is a home that is lived in by DeFranceschi's.» The names of the people living in it are omitted here under this archive's rule on the living.

album.provenance: The album records its own chain of custody, which is worth having. A man who had married into the house more than fifty years before, and who turned ninety in 2013, handed over his handwritten notes of the family tree and asked for them to be finished before that birthday. A cousin had made a tape of the family genealogy years earlier and passed it round. Another cousin had been researching the family in the 1970s. The album was assembled in about two months. Those three things — the handwritten notes, the tape and the 1970s research — are in family hands somewhere, and any one of them would be worth more to this archive than another week in the newspapers.
album.cousins: What the chart means for this line, stated plainly. The Antonio at the head of it, born 6 August 1856, is the eldest son of Antonio the stonecutter of house 19 and his wife Maria née Fernasar — and the elder brother of Josip, born 22 March 1863, who took this archive's own line down to Crikvenica. So the eleven children of the chart are the first cousins of this line's Anton Rudolf, and everyone at the Crystal Springs reunion in 2012 was a cousin of the people this site is written for. The two halves of the family last shared a household at Gračišće in the 1860s, and then one went to the Kvarner, Germany, South Africa and Australia, and the other to New York, Buenos Aires and Tuscany.
album.note_date: One thing to check in the register rather than assume. This archive's own reading of the Gračišće books gives Antonio the stonecutter's marriage to Maria Fernasar as 25 November 1856, and his eldest son Antonius as born on 6 August 1856 — three and a half months earlier. Either a child was legitimated by his parents' subsequent marriage, which is common enough and would be noted in the margin, or one of the two dates has been read wrong here. The entries exist and would settle it.

gracisce.heading: And one of the eleven is still in the ground at Gračišće
gracisce.lead: The album and its chart were read here this morning. This afternoon the family walked into the cemetery at Gračišće and photographed the plot — and the instruction that came with the pictures was to look at the middle stone. It is the right instruction. The middle stone is the parents.
gracisce.quote: F. DE FRANCESCHI — MARFAN — VIRGINIJA ✱ 30. III. 1895 ✝ 28. XII. 1981 — NAZARIJO ✱ 7. 02. 1939 ✝ 11. 12. 2003

rows.lab: Virginija de Franceschi Marfan, 30 March 1895 – 28 December 1981
rows.text: The chart printed for the Crystal Springs reunion in 2012 gives «VIRGINIA (3/30/1895)», sixth of the eleven children of Antonio DeFranceschi and Maria Valhart, and the album says she married Giovanni Marfan and had four children. The stone gives 30 March 1895. Same day, same month, same year — one written down in America in 2012, the other cut in Istria in 1981. And it gives what the chart did not: she died on 28 December 1981, aged eighty-six, and she is buried in her own village.

rows.lab: Nazarijo Marfan, 7 February 1939 – 11 December 2003
rows.text: The chart gives «Nazario (2/7/1939)» as one of her four. The stone gives 7 February 1939. He is the man the album remembers: the writer first came to Gallignana in 1972 and was received by Aunt Virginia; years later «her son Nazario and his wife Mila» gave the visiting American cousins lunch and their own wine, and the afternoon went under the grape arbour. He died on 11 December 2003.

rows.lab: And the name on the stone is written twice over
rows.text: «F. DE FRANCESCHI» at the head — the family — and «MARFAN» beneath it, the name the daughter married into. Two porcelain ovals are set into the marble, an older woman and a man in a suit and tie. It is the same convention as the Carnian stones at Santa Maria di Gorto, where six of the eleven De Franceschi graves are a daughter under her husband's name.

rows.lab: The middle stone: Antonio and Maria themselves
rows.text: A cross-topped obelisk stands between the Salamon and Marfan monuments, and it reads «ANTONIO DEFRANCESCHI 185[5 or 6] – 19[2]4» and «MARIA DEFRANCESCHI 6. IV. 1867 – 3. X. 1945». These are the two names at the head of the American chart — «started by Antonio DeFranceschi 8/6/1856 – 10/23/1924 + Maria Valhart 4/6/1867 – 1945». The chart is in American date order, so its 4/6/1867 is the sixth of April, and the stone says 6.IV.1867. A date written down in California in 2012 and a date cut in Istria after 1945, and they agree exactly. And the stone gives what the chart could not: Maria died on 3 October 1945. The chart had only the year.

rows.lab: What the stone does not settle
rows.text: Antonio's line is worn, and reads 185[5 or 6] to 19[2]4. That is consistent with the chart's 6 August 1856 and 23 October 1924 and does nothing to contradict it, but it is not independent confirmation — the digits that would confirm are the ones the weather has taken. It is the single most valuable surface in that cemetery for this archive, and it wants one photograph in raking light. Note also that the stone calls her MARIA DEFRANCESCHI, not Valhart: on her own husband's monument she carries his name, and the maiden name survives only on the American chart and in the registers.

gracisce.why: Why this matters more than one more grave. Virginija was the niece of Josip Defranceschi — the stonecutter's son who took this archive's own line down to Crikvenica in 1890 — and therefore the first cousin of Anton Rudolf. The two halves of the family parted at Gračišće in the 1860s. One went to the Kvarner, Germany, South Africa and Australia. The other went to New York, Buenos Aires and Tuscany — except this one, who stayed, married a Marfan, and was still receiving her American cousins in the family house in the 1970s. Her son was the last of them in it. He died in 2003, and the archive has the date because somebody drove there and read it off the stone.
gracisce.source_gracisce: Photographed by the family at the Gračišće cemetery, 2026, and read image by image. Compared against «The Generations of DeFranceschi (2012)», the chart printed for the family reunion at Crystal Springs. The other surnames standing with them in that ground — Salamon, Marfan, Grubišić, Lanča, Buršić, Vojsković, Laginja, Fornažar, Milanović, Vlahović — are recorded in the archive's files but are not published here except where they touch this family.
gracisce.gathered: One more thing the plot says by its arrangement. Four monuments stand together: the Coniugi stone of Rosa Ivich and Silvio Salamon with their son Ottavio and Bruno Salamon; the F. SALAMON stone of Franjo and Marija; the obelisk of Antonio and Maria DeFranceschi; and the F. DE FRANCESCHI — MARFAN stone of their daughter Virginija and her son Nazarijo. A second Marfan monument stands elsewhere in the cemetery. And the F. MARFAN stone beside the obelisk, for Mafalda and Ivan, is dedicated «GENITORI, FRATELLO E SORELLE POSERO» — set up by parents, brother and sisters, in Italian, in a cemetery where almost every other stone of those years is in Croatian. The archive has long had Virginija marrying a Marfan. What the plot shows is that the two families buried together, and that the Salamon are in with them — the same Salamon whose Francisca married into this line at Gračišće in 1819.

register.heading: And then the parish register produced all of them, with dates
register.lead: The eleven children of the American chart have been on this site as a chart — names and years typed up in California in 2012 out of family memory. The Gračišće Status Animarum of 1925, photographed on a reading-room screen at Pazin and read image by image, gives house 24, and in it the whole household, in the parish priest's hand.

rows.lab: The parents
rows.text: «Antonius Defranceschi q. Antonii, murator, 6-8-1856, m. 23-2-1885, † 23-10-1929» and «Maria n. Volhardt, eius uxor, 6-4-1867». A mason. Married on 23 February 1885 — the day digit is 23 and not 25, read again at full magnification against the same hand's threes elsewhere on the page. And his wife's birth date is 6 April 1867 — which is exactly what the obelisk in the Gračišće cemetery says, «MARIA DEFRANCESCHI 6. IV. 1867 – 3. X. 1945», and exactly what the American chart says as 4/6/1867. Three independent records, one date.

rows.lab: And the children, all of them
rows.text: Antonius 18-2-1887, married 31-5-1919 · Paschalis 1-4-1888, died 16-10-1895 · Nicephorus 1-1-1890 · Josephus 12-3-1892 · Virginia 30-5-1895 · Victoria-Ema 16-2-1898, died 14-5-1902 · Albina 14-4-1900 · Rutilius 3-11-1902, married 16-5-1928 · Daniel 8-3-1905, married 2-7-1927 · Joachim 12-8-1907 · **Basilius 29-9-1909, married 28-2-1936**. Thirteen born, two dead in childhood, eleven who grew up. The chart said eleven and the register says why.

rows.lab: Three of them marked «degit Americae»
rows.text: Against Nicephorus, against Albina and against Joachim the priest has written that they were living in America. He was keeping a running note of where his parishioners had gone.

rows.lab: Which closes the Conte Rosso
rows.text: The manifest of the S.S. Conte Rosso, Genoa to New York, 29 August 1922, carries «DE FRANCESCHI ALBINA, 22, domestic, Venezia G. Gallignana, Father Antonio — Gallignano». This page had her as one of the eleven and could not prove the father. The register gives Albina born 14 April 1900 at Gračišće, daughter of Antonius the mason, and marks her as gone to America. She was twenty-two in August 1922. It is the same woman, and her father is the man on the obelisk.

rows.lab: One date that does not agree
rows.text: The American chart gives Antonio's death as 10/23/1924 — 23 October 1924. The parish register gives 25-10-1929. Two days apart in the day and five years apart in the year, which is a strange kind of disagreement and probably means one of them is a transcription of the other gone wrong. The worn obelisk reads 19[2]4 and cannot arbitrate. The Gračišće civil death register would.

rows.lab: And which also closes Basilio
rows.text: Basilius is the last name in the column, and his birth date is **29 September 1909** — read at full magnification, where the month digit is a nine and not the three this page first printed. The Diaspora page of this archive has carried, for months, a New York family it could describe and could not place: «DEFRANCESCHI, DARIO, also known as DARIO DE FRANCESCH, was born 26 September 1937 in GALLIGNANA, Austria, son of BASILIO DEFRANCESCHI and MARIA L ROVINA» — and a father Basilio born **29 September 1909**, who took a New York social security number, made his claim at the Jackson Heights office in 1971, and died in Manhattan on 15 June 1994. That page ended: «Nothing yet joins Basilio to this line.» Something does now. The day, the month and the year are the same, the parish is the same, and the register adds the step in between — Basilius married on **28 February 1936**, eighteen months before Dario was born at Gallignana. He is the youngest of the thirteen children of Antonio the mason and Maria Volhardt: the twelfth name under the household that this page has always called the Eleven.

register.further: The same read gives the generation above, and it is this archive's own line. Gračišće Status Animarum 1870, house 19: «Antonius Defranceschi, lapidarius» — stonecutter — «born 20 September 1825, married 25 November 1856 Maria n. Fernasar, born 17 October 1832», with their children Antonius 1856, Josephus 1863 and the rest. And the Škopljaci book of 1841, house 5, gives that Antonius as a son: «Joan. Bapt. Defranceschi, agricola, born 13 August 1787, married 1819 Francisca Salomon, died 14 September 1846», and among his children «Antonius, 20 7bris 1825». So the stonecutter's father is named, with a birth date of 13 August 1787 — which is the very date this archive's research log has been carrying as an open question, asking whether the head of Gračišće house 5 was the boy baptised at Gologorica house 31 on 13 August 1787. He is at house 5. The question is now half closed and the Gologorica end of it is the half that remains.
register.scale: That is two households out of a much larger harvest. The Pazin screens the family photographed carry, between them, something over ninety distinct people of this surname — the Gologorica Status Animarum of 1894 for houses 2, 7, 8, 11 and 87, the Gračišće books of 1841, 1865, 1870 and 1925, and the parish's own alphabetical repertorium with its death dates and page references. They have been transcribed and they are not yet all published. That is the next substantial piece of work on this site.
register.source_reg: Državni arhiv u Pazinu, Status Animarum: Gračišće 1925 (ZM 34K-219, M01072529–M01072929), Gračišće 1870 and 1865 (ZM 34K-218), Gračišće–Škopljaci 1841 (ZM 34K-218, M01072065–M01072218), Gologorica 1894 (ZM 34K-215, M01069580–M01069825). Photographed from the reading-room screens by the family, autumn 2026, and read image by image. Where the register gives an age at death in years, months and days, the arithmetic has been checked against the birth date; it matches every time, and that is what settled several ambiguous digits.

before.heading: Antonio was born before his parents married, and his mother was born outside marriage too
before.lead: The household books have been read twice over by different readers, and the second pass turned up something the chart printed in California could not have carried. It is not a scandal. It is the ordinary shape of a poor family's life in an Istrian village, written down plainly by a priest who saw no reason to hide it.

rows.lab: The grandmother
rows.text: House 21, and again house 20: «Catharina Fernasar, agr., 1800», and beneath her «Maria, filia ejus illegitima, 17 Oct. 1832» — Maria, her illegitimate daughter. A second child, Joannes, is entered the same way. So Maria née Fernasar, who married the stonecutter, was herself born outside marriage.

rows.lab: And her eldest son
rows.text: The same page carries, under house 20, «Antonius, filius illeg. Mariae, 6 Aug. 1856» — Antonius, illegitimate son of Maria. The marriage of Antonius Defranceschi the stonecutter to Maria Fernasar is dated 25 November 1856. Her son was born on 6 August, fifteen weeks earlier. When they married he was legitimised, and from then on every register enters him as their son.

rows.lab: That son is the man at the head of the chart
rows.text: Antonius, born 6 August 1856, the mason — «Antonio DeFranceschi 8/6/1856» at the top of the chart printed for the Crystal Springs reunion in 2012, husband of Maria Valhart, father of the eleven children. He was born three and a half months before his parents' wedding, to a mother who had herself been born outside marriage twenty-four years earlier.

rows.lab: And his wife came out of an orphanage
rows.text: Against Maria née Volhardt, whom he married on 23 February 1889, the priest wrote «nata in Orphanotrophio Tergesti» — born in the orphanage at Trieste. So the couple at the head of the American chart were an illegitimately-born mason from a village of four hundred people and a foundling from a Trieste institution, and between them they had thirteen children, eleven of whom grew up, and four of those went to America.

rows.lab: Why this is published
rows.text: Because it is true and because the parish priest wrote it without embarrassment in a book meant to be read by his successors. A family archive that quietly rounded these edges off would be doing something the people in it did not do. The entries are matter-of-fact: illegitima, illeg. Mariae, nata in Orphanotrophio. Nobody was hiding anything, and a hundred and seventy years later there is nothing here to be ashamed of and a good deal to be moved by.

before.source_before: Državni arhiv u Pazinu, Status Animarum of Gologorica and Gračišće, houses 19, 20, 21 and 24, photographed by the family and read image by image, twice, by separate readers. The 1889 marriage date and Maria Volhardt's birthplace are from the house-24 page.

america.heading: The household reassembles in Brooklyn — and Rotilio does not
america.lead: The register gave the thirteen births. The American record now gives what happened to them, and it is more concentrated than anyone had assumed: **five of the eleven can be documented in New York**, four of them in Brooklyn, and the mason's wife's maiden name — which no chart outside the family carries — appears on three separate American documents. It also removes the one detail that held Rotilio's story together.

rows.lab: Albina's death certificate, and why it matters more than the rest
rows.text:
New York City, **27 April 1945**: «Albina Chinkopan», died at **Brooklyn**, born **14 April 1900 in Austria**, buried **30 April 1945** at East Farmingdale in Suffolk County. The certificate names her parents. **Father: Anthony De Franceschi, born Austria. Mother: Maria Walhart, born Austria.**

«Walhart» is **Volhardt** — the name the Gračišće priest wrote in the Status Animarum of 1925 as «Maria n. Volhardt, eius uxor, 6-4-1867». An American registrar heard it and spelt it as he heard it. **That single misspelling is the proof**: it ties a Brooklyn death certificate to house 24 at Gračišće without any inference at all.

rows.lab: So the marriage runs the other way
rows.text:
This page has carried, out of the 2012 reunion album, that **Rotilio married Albina Chinkopan**, «the sister, presumably, of his own sister's husband». It is now clear that there was **only ever one Albina and one Chinkopan marriage**, and it is the sister's. Albina De Franceschi, born 14 April 1900, married **Frank Chinkopan** — himself born at **Gallignana in 1896–97**, so a boy from the same village — and the pair of them naturalised in New York, she on **5 April 1928**. He died at **Manhattan on 7 May 1948**, three years after her; his own parents were Anthony and Maria Linpich. His brother **Antonio Chinkopan**, born at Gallignana in August 1898, naturalised at Brooklyn in the early 1930s and married a Jennie born in Brooklyn in 1911.

**Which means the album gave Rotilio his sister's husband's surname.** The one concrete detail attached to him — the name of his wife — is a duplication.

rows.lab: And Rotilio himself is not in Argentina
rows.text:
Searched properly rather than gestured at. **«Rotilio» as a given name in Argentine records** returns a dozen men — Voltolini, Cichini, Moreira, Ballesteros, Jurado, Juarez — and **not one of them carries this surname**. **The surname in Argentina** between 1900 and 1910 returns another dozen — Piergiacomi, Rosso, Oreste, Adolfo, Ernesto at La Plata and La Boca — an Italian-mainland stock with Italian-mainland in-law names, and **no Rotilio among them**. Nothing in the United States either.

What the parish register does give is a man: **«Rutilius 3-11-1902, married 16-5-1928»** — born 3 November 1902, not 1903, and **married at sixteen May 1928**, five years after the last of his brothers had sailed. The priest marked Nicephorus, Albina and Joachim as «degit Americae». **He did not mark Rutilius.** As of 1928 he was at home, and getting married there.

rows.lab: Where that leaves the Argentina claim
rows.text: Weaker than it was this morning, and the diagram says so. The album's Buenos Aires rests on family memory alone; its supporting detail turns out to belong to his sister; and the register shows him in Istria six years after the album's own emigration window. **This is not a claim that he never went.** Two daughters and a destination are the kind of thing families remember correctly, and CEMLA's arrival index — the one instrument that would answer it — is behind a bot check this archive will not answer. But the honest position is that **Rotilio is now the least evidenced of the eleven**, and Argentina stays dotted.

rows.lab: The four who are certain
rows.text: **Antonio «Tony»**, born 18 February 1887 — naturalised at **Brooklyn on 18 September 1922 and again 10 April 1929**, with a wife Marta born 1894. *This page had him in Italy; he was in Brooklyn.* **Giuseppe**, born 12 March 1892 — naturalisations of **2 February 1912** and 13 December 1915, the earliest of the family in America by a decade. **Gioacchino «Bruno»**, born 12 August 1907 — naturalised at **Brooklyn on 18 April 1945**, with **Gerda Seedorf**, born Hanover; his record names his parents as «Anton» and «Mary Walhal» — Volhardt again, spelt differently again. **Basilio**, born 29 September 1909 — at Jackson Heights, with Maria Rovina and his son Dario, born at Gallignana 26 September 1937.

rows.lab: What this adds up to
rows.text: Antonio the mason and Maria Volhardt raised thirteen children in one house at Gračišće. Two died small. **Of the eleven who grew up, five reached New York and four of them lived within a few miles of each other in Brooklyn**, alongside at least two Chinkopan brothers from the same village. Virginia stayed and received the American cousins at Gallignana in 1972. Daniele went to Tuscany in 1947. Pasquale and Nicefaro left young and were never heard from. And Rotilio married in 1928 and then, on the present evidence, vanishes.

america.source_am: United States naturalization records for the Eastern District of New York and the Southern District of New York; New York City death certificates (Albina Chinkopan, 27 April 1945; Frank Chinkopan, 7 May 1948); the United States federal censuses of 1940 and 1950; and the Social Security Numident. All read through the FamilySearch record indexes, September 2026, in David Defranceski's own signed-in session. The Argentine negative was run against the same index for Argentina; CEMLA's own arrival database was not searched, because it is behind a bot check. The Gračišće Status Animarum of 1925, house 24, is this archive's own photograph.
